subsystems.name: Precursor molecules
subsystems.role: the monomers that decide a ribbon's width and edge shape before the ribbon exists.

subsystems.name: Growth surface and vacuum
subsystems.role: an atomically flat metal surface in ultra-high vacuum where the ribbons are assembled.

subsystems.name: Coupling and fusion chemistry
subsystems.role: two heat-driven reactions that stitch monomers into a solid ribbon.

subsystems.name: Transfer and alignment
subsystems.role: moving ribbons off the metal onto the insulating surface a device needs, in a known direction.

subsystems.name: Characterisation
subsystems.role: proving the ribbon really has the width and edge structure that was designed.

subsystems.name: Device fabrication
subsystems.role: turning one or a few ribbons into a working transistor or sensor.

buildSteps.title: Design the monomer
buildSteps.detail: Chemists pick a molecule whose shape sets the final width. Armchair edges give a bandgap that shrinks as the ribbon widens; zigzag edges carry magnetic edge states.

buildSteps.title: Synthesise the precursor
buildSteps.detail: The monomer is built by ordinary organic chemistry in solution, then purified — this is where the atomic precision comes from.

buildSteps.title: Deposit on a metal surface
buildSteps.detail: The powder is heated in vacuum so it sublimes onto a clean single-crystal gold or copper surface, forming less than a full covering of molecules.

buildSteps.title: Couple the monomers
buildSteps.detail: Mild heating breaks the halogen caps and links neighbouring molecules into chains, with the metal surface acting as catalyst.

buildSteps.title: Fuse into a ribbon
buildSteps.detail: Hotter heating drives cyclodehydrogenation: the remaining carbon–hydrogen bonds close, fusing the chain into a flat, fully aromatic ribbon.

buildSteps.title: Inspect
buildSteps.detail: Scanning tunnelling microscopy images the result atom by atom, confirming width, edge type and where defects crept in.

buildSteps.title: Transfer onto an insulator
buildSteps.detail: Because the growth metal conducts, ribbons must be lifted onto a dielectric before they can switch a current on and off.

buildSteps.title: Build the device
buildSteps.detail: Electrodes, a gate dielectric and an encapsulating layer are added to make a transistor or a sensor, then tested.

prerequisites.why: the coupling and cyclisation reactions are established laboratory technique.
scanning probe imaging is the only routine way to confirm a ribbon's width and edges.
decades of graphene and nanotube work supply transfer, contacting and encapsulation know-how.
today's synthesis yields tiny amounts on small chips, not the quantities a factory needs.
there is no routine way to put millions of identical, aligned ribbons exactly where a chip needs them.
oxides trap charge and scatter carriers, so ribbons on insulators need careful passivation.

pathway.milestone: laboratory ribbons with precisely chosen widths and edges; single-ribbon transistors and sensors demonstrated
pathway.unlocks: proof that quantum confinement can give graphene a usable bandgap.

pathway.milestone: growth or placement directly on insulating and semiconducting substrates, with ribbons aligned rather than scattered
wafer-scale arrays of a single ribbon type, integrated into test circuits
pathway.unlocks: real comparison against silicon and other channel materials.

pathway.milestone: ribbons as transistor channels below a few nanometres wide, as chemical sensors, and as hosts for spin-based quantum bits
pathway.unlocks: electronics that keeps shrinking once silicon reaches its limits — if placement, yield and lifetime are solved.
